title: The LORD's Case Against Israel
overview: The LORD brings a courtroom charge against the northern kingdom of Israel, blaming its priests most of all for a people who have forgotten God and turned to idols.

parts.label: The charges laid out (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Like a lawyer in court, the LORD accuses Israel of having no honesty, no loyal love and no real knowledge of God, only lying, murder, theft and adultery that echo the broken Ten Commandments. The constant bloodshed likely reflects a string of murdered kings in this period, and even the land, animals and fish are pictured wasting away.

parts.label: Priests who failed (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: Verse 4 is unclear in the Hebrew, but the point seems to be that blaming ordinary people is useless when priests and prophets have stumbled too; "your mother" stands for the nation itself. Priests were meant to teach God's ways, so because they threw that knowledge away, God rejects them and their descendants as priests.

parts.label: Profiting from sin (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Priests ate part of the animals people offered to make up for wrongdoing, so more sin meant more food for them, and they came to want it. Priest and people will share the same judgment: they will eat and stay hungry, and their unfaithfulness will not bring the children they hope for.

parts.label: Worship on the hilltops (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: People sought guidance from wooden idols and a diviner's stick used to read omens, and held drunken worship at shady hilltop shrines linked to Canaanite gods. God will not single out the young women caught up in this, since the men set the example by going off with women at the shrines; scholars debate whether this means actual ritual sex or is mainly a picture of unfaithfulness to God.

parts.label: A warning to Judah (vv. 15-19)
parts.note: Judah, the southern kingdom, is told not to copy the north at Gilgal or Bethel, old holy places now used for mixed worship; "Beth Aven," meaning "house of wickedness," mocks Bethel, "house of God." Ephraim, another name for the north, is like a cow refusing the yoke and will be carried off by the wind, likely pointing to coming exile under Assyria.

think: When the people meant to guide a community quietly benefit from its failures, how much of the blame do you think falls on them rather than on everyone else?
